opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to where the leverage is. Right now, if you take the current models and point them at open problems in math or physics, you can get some really interesting results. We've seen models help with proofs, find counterexamples, and do a lot of the grunt work that researchers used to spend weeks on. That's exciting, and I don't want to downplay it.

But if you think about the trajectory, the models a year from now are going to be dramatically better than the models today. If you spent a huge amount of effort and compute squeezing every last result out of the current generation, a lot of that work would be superseded almost immediately. The next model might solve in an afternoon the problem you spent six months engineering a pipeline around. So from a pure opportunity-cost perspective, pushing the frontier of capability tends to pay off more than optimizing applications of a model that's about to be obsolete.

There's also a generality argument. When we improve reasoning, longer-horizon thinking, and the ability to verify its own work, that doesn't just help with one theorem or one physics question. It helps across every domain at once. Solving a specific open problem is great, but it's a single data point. Building a model that's fundamentally better at reasoning unlocks thousands of those.

That said, it's not either/or. Working on hard open problems is a really useful signal. It tells you where the models break down, what kinds of reasoning they're still missing, and it gives you a much better evaluation than saturated benchmarks. So I'd frame it as: the primary goal should be making the models more capable, and engaging with frontier science is one of the best ways to figure out what "more capable" actually needs to mean. And frankly, I think the most impressive scientific results are going to come almost as a byproduct once the models get good enough. We're close to that point, so it makes sense to keep our eye on making them better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses applying current models to open science problems, but does not present making models available to scientists worldwide so they can solve those problems themselves.

r002.rationale: It advocates improving model capability, but does not say to use existing AI models to develop more capable models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a bit of a false dichotomy baked into that question, and I want to push on it a little before I answer it directly.

The way I think about it is: if you take a model at some fixed level of capability and you throw it at the hardest open problems in math or physics, you're going to get some amount of progress. Maybe you crack a few things, maybe you make incremental headway on a few more. But that progress is capped by what the model can do today. And historically, the lesson of the last several years has been that a more capable model doesn't just do the same things slightly better. It opens up entire categories of problems that were completely out of reach before.

So if I imagine spending the next two years with all our best researchers and compute pointed at, say, the Riemann hypothesis using today's models, versus spending that time making the models fundamentally better and then pointing them at Riemann, I'm pretty confident the second path gets you further. Not just on Riemann, but on everything. The capability work compounds in a way that direct application doesn't.

There's also an efficiency argument. A lot of what the model learns in the process of becoming more capable is general. It's not Riemann-specific. So when you make the model better at reasoning, you're not just making progress on one open problem, you're making progress on thousands of them simultaneously. That's a much higher-leverage use of a scarce resource.

Now, I'll give you the caveat, because I don't think it's actually either-or. You do need to be testing these models against real, hard, open problems. Partly because that's how you find out where they fall down, and that tells you what to fix. And partly because, honestly, if a model can make a genuine contribution to mathematics or physics, you should let it. That's enormously valuable in its own right, and it's a signal to the world about where we are. So I don't want to say "never apply the models." I want to say: the primary objective should be capability, and the applications are both a byproduct and a diagnostic.

The last thing I'd add is that I think a lot of people underestimate how early we still are. There's a temptation when the models get impressive to say, okay, let's stop and harvest. But the trajectory we're on suggests there's a lot more headroom, and the cost of pausing on that curve to pick the fruit that's currently reachable is just much higher than people appreciate. The fruit that becomes reachable a couple of years from now is going to be a lot more interesting.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues for improving models and testing them on open problems, but does not present making models available to scientists worldwide so they can solve those problems themselves.

r002.rationale: The candidate advocates making models more capable, but does not say to use existing AI models to develop those more capable models.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a question of where you get the most leverage. You could take the models we have today and put a lot of effort into getting them to solve a particular open problem. That would be valuable. But if that same effort goes toward building a more capable model, you might end up with something that can solve that problem and a whole range of other problems as well.

There’s also a feedback loop: more capable models can help us do the research that makes the next generation better. So the benefit isn’t just a better tool for mathematics or physics; it’s potentially accelerating the process of developing those tools.

That doesn’t mean we should ignore applications. Trying to solve real scientific problems is a great way to understand what’s missing from our models. But while we’re still making substantial progress on general capabilities, I think that’s where a lot of the research effort should go.

r001.rationale: The response does not say to make models available to scientists worldwide so they can solve open mathematics and physics problems themselves.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop in which more capable models help research that improves the next generation of models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest argument is that improving the models is a way to accelerate all of those problems at once. You could put a lot of effort into getting today’s models to solve one particular open problem, and that would be valuable. But if the same effort gets you to a model that’s substantially better at research, you may then be able to make progress on many problems in mathematics and physics.

There’s also a feedback loop: better models can help us do the research that produces the next generation of models. That makes capability research potentially very high leverage.

I wouldn’t make it an absolute choice, though. Trying to solve real scientific problems is a great way to find out what the models are missing. You want that feedback. But I’d put the emphasis on building the general research capability, rather than spending a huge amount of effort engineering around the limitations of a particular model.

r001.rationale: The response argues for improving general research capability, but does not say to make models available to scientists worldwide so they can solve problems themselves.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop in which better models help conduct research that produces the next generation of models, supporting the use of AI models to develop more capable ones.
